text.p: The price of copper traded above the important psychological threshold of $2,000 a tonne on Thursday for the first time in seven weeks.
Copper had languished on fears that a stockpile hoarded by disgraced star trader Yasuo Hamanaka of Japan had yet to be fully unloaded.

Hamanaka faces forgery charges after employers Sumitomo Corp said he was a maverick who lost it $2.6 billion. But falling stocks of copper and also rising U.S. offtake of aluminium lured both the industrial and speculator fraternities back to the London Metal Exchange this week.
As copper in late trading hit $2,000, London aluminium also gained about $20 to break resistance at $1,420 a tonne.

LME floor traders said copper rose in anticipation of another sizeable drawdown in LME copper stocks on Friday. Stocks have fallen over 115,000 tonnes in less than two months and are not far above the low point of 141,100 reached in July 1995.
It was being shipped to end-users in Europe and the Middle East as well as to China, traders said.
Although stocks were low and expected to fall further, doubts remained over the market's upside potential as producers appeared keen to sell into any rise.
Aluminium traders were encouraged by U.S. Aluminium Association data showing demand in the world's biggest market up by 8.5 percent in August from the previous month.
Analysts were also citing trade talk of the possibility of a meeting of leading producers in Moscow, to discuss the current statistical situation of the market, as potentially bullish.

Aluminium finished above previous resistance at $1,420 while other metals moved in tandem with market leaders copper and aluminium in fairly thin volumes, traders and analysts said. Nickel gained $55 to $7,230 while zinc rose $2.50 to $1,027. Lead edged up $2 to $737 and alloy moved to $1,280 from $1,270. Tin was the only metal to buck the trend, nudging lower by $5 to $5,980 by the close.

A surprising hike in the EU's export subsidy for wheat and wheat flour plus a dismal weekly U.S. wheat export sales pace dropped CBOT wheat futures sharply lower on the close, traders said. New lows were set, selling was broad-based and included commercial selling plus unwinding of CBOT/KCBT and CBOT/MGE wheat spreads, the traders said. The new low for March was $3.79, down from the previous low of $3.87-1/2 set Tuesday. Grain exporters said EU officials in Brussels had awarded wheat export subsidies up to 13 Ecus per tonne for 290,000 tonnes of wheat, stretching into double figures for the first time this season and raising market competition another notch. Wheat collapsed late with fund, commission house, local and commercial selling noted during the last 15 minutes of trading. Wheat closed 1-1/2 to 14-1/2 cents per bushel lower, with December down 14-1/2 at $3.84.

A drop in Ukraine's expecations for its 1996/97 sugar output to 2.8 million tonnes from 3.2 million previously helped steady a previous lacklustre sugar market. Nearby London white sugar futures gave up much of their modest gains by the close after a day of thin trading. December -- responsible for 193 lots of the paltry 425-lot total volume -- ended 50 cents higher at $316.70 per tonne after trading as high as $318.50. March closed unchanged at $313.50. Trade buying had offered earlier support, but volumes remained thin as Sugar Week comes to an end. In Paris, December ended 10 cents easier at $316.50 and March 60 cents higher at $314.20.

New York precious metals futures ended lower, giving back some of the gains seen earlier this week, and raising doubts about whether the downtrend since early September was over. COMEX December gold ended down $1.00 an ounce at $384.90, after finding some support at the intraday lows at $384.50. In bullion trade, spot gold ended quoted $382.85/383.25, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $383.00 and the New York close Wednesday at $383.60/384.10.
